title: Daughter Zion
lead: A city or people pictured as a daughter: Zion, Judah and Jerusalem most often, and also Babylon and Edom. Lamentations uses it more than any other book.

sections.b: In Hebrew the "daughter of" before a city's name is a kind of title: the city, thought of as a young woman. Isaiah calls Zion a hut in a vineyard (Isaiah 1:8), the daughter whom the king of Assyria cannot frighten (Isaiah 37:22), and the one who is told to rejoice (Zechariah 2:10; 9:9). Micah 4:8-10 has her cry out in labor; Jeremiah hears her cry (Jeremiah 4:31). Foreign cities are daughters too: the virgin daughter of Babylon in Isaiah 47:1, the daughter of Babylon in Psalm 137:8, the daughter of Edom in Lamentations 4:21-22.
sections.refs: Isaiah 1:8; Isaiah 37:22; Isaiah 47:1; Micah 4:8; Jeremiah 4:31; Zechariah 2:10; Zechariah 9:9; Psalm 137:8

sections.b: In Lamentations the daughter is a widow (1:1), an unfaithful wife (1:8), a mother who has lost her children (1:16), a woman stripped and mocked (1:8; 2:15) and a daughter told to cry out in the night (2:18-19). "The daughter of my people" (rendered "my dear people" in the Plain English Translation) is the same pattern, as in Jeremiah 8:11. Scholars differ on the source of the image: Dobbs-Allsopp argues that it comes from the weeping city-goddess of Mesopotamian laments; others point to the Hebrew habit of speaking of a place as a woman.
